title: Wavelength and the Pre-GenAI Legal-Engineering Model (2016-2021)
pub: SRA; Law Society Gazette; Society for Computers and Law Student Bytes
author: Solicitors Regulation Authority · Katharine Freeland · Ryan Fong · Will Lilley

dom.t: Regulated delivery: Wavelength predates generative AI transformation

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts legal engineering as an implementation bridge and materially develops the cluster by identifying learnable technical and data-oriented skills, alongside client education, as practical capabilities needed to translate technology into usable legal services. Its contribution is experience-based rather than evidence of improved reliability or outcomes.
qs: Let this spill into the way you view and understand the law, since this is something you'll need in order to succeed as a legal engineer.
All this means is that we have to put more effort making people and our clients aware of what is available and how they can deploy these technologies in the best way possible.

st.t: Regulated delivery: Wavelength predates generative AI transformation
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis by documenting Wavelength as an SRA-licensed legal-services body since 2016, with differentiated solicitor and nonlawyer compliance roles and qualified regulatory protections. It provides institutional evidence but no evidence of generative-AI transformation, productivity outcomes or comprehensive assurance.
qs: London + 3 other offices    View contact details           Website   www.wavelength.law        Type of firm   Licensed body since 01/06/2016, authorised for all legal services        Regulator   Solicitors Regulation Authority        SRA number   629796        Company registration    9996604        Regulatory record     No decisions published.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s operating-model redesign proposition by presenting legal engineers as the bridge between legal expertise, technology and solution design, and by illustrating their use in a concrete contract-review workflow. It also claims substantial task-level efficiency benefits. However, as a pre-GenAI account, it does not substantively address jagged capability, verification burdens or selective deployment by risk and task.
qs: ‘They are people who advise on, develop and create solutions, and are essential in keeping firms ahead of the curve.’   In recent weeks legal engineers have been using the platforms that Hogan Lovells built to review force majeure clauses in contracts that could be triggered by the global Covid-19 shutdown.
It makes legal processes quicker, more efficient and accurate at a fraction of the time, cost and manpower previously required.

kp.k: Regulated legal engineering preceded generative AI
kp.d: The SRA register records Simmons Wavelength as a licensed body authorised for all legal services since 01/06/2016. The interview's accompanying profile dates its establishment to 2016 and acquisition by Simmons & Simmons to summer 2019. Freeland reports Wavelength's claim to be the world's first SRA-regulated legal engineering business; that priority claim is distinct from the register's confirmation of authorisation.
qs: Licensed body since 01/06/2016, authorised for all legal services
Established in 2016, the business was acquired by Simmons & Simmons in the summer of 2019.
Wavelength claims to be the world’s first Solicitors Regulation Authority-regulated legal engineering business.

kp.k: Legal engineers translate between legal and technical expertise
kp.d: Freeland's May 2020 feature describes an emerging role combining legal-process understanding with technology expertise. Hogan Lovells' Stephen Allen likens legal engineers to solutions architects, while Will Lilley describes his own role as understanding Simmons & Simmons teams' procedures and linking lawyers with data scientists to improve service delivery.
qs: Legal engineers are similar to what other industries would call “solutions architects”
In my role, I work with different teams at Simmons & Simmons to understand their internal procedures in order to optimise and improve the way they deliver legal services.
Considering my legal background and passion for technology, you can also say that I act as a link between lawyers and data scientists.

kp.k: Process redesign anchors Wavelength's service offering
kp.d: Lilley identifies modelling and implementing robust legal processes, rather than selling a particular technology, as Wavelength's core service. He describes identifying inefficiencies in everyday work and having data scientists turn lawyers' ideas into personalised coded solutions.
qs: The key service we provide is modelling and implementing a robust legal process.
In other words, we work out what somebody does day-to-day, find the cracks in terms of efficiency and improve them.
A simple example is when our legal engineers relay the ideas of lawyers in the field to data scientists who use code to stitch together personalised solutions.

kp.k: Small multidisciplinary teams support iterative client delivery
kp.d: Lilley reports that Wavelength uses project teams of five to six people, potentially combining legal engineers, data scientists, technologists, lawyers and designers. He attributes continuous communication and rapid personalisation in response to client feedback to this scrum-based organisation; these are practitioner claims rather than measured comparative findings.
qs: We have "scrums", which are small teams of five to six people working together on a specific project for a client.
The teams often include legal engineers, data scientists, technologists, lawyers and designers.
Moreover, this allows us to easily and quickly personalise the final product based on client feedback.

kp.k: Technology agnosticism combines market knowledge and bespoke capabilities
kp.d: Lilley says Wavelength is not tied to any technology provider and selects solutions around client needs, requiring extensive knowledge of available technologies. The accompanying profile states that legal engineers can also deploy bespoke code and proprietary in-house AI where necessary; it does not identify those capabilities as generative AI.
qs: Furthermore, we are technology agnostic which means we’re not tethered to any provider.
We don’t push any commercial interest other than the best solution for our client.
Its legal engineers are also able to deploy bespoke code and proprietary, in-house artificial intelligence capabilities where necessary.

kp.k: Projects target diligence, litigation evidence and fund administration
kp.d: The interview introduction reports three examples of Lilley's recent work: redesigning corporate M&A due diligence, iteratively producing reports from client legal data and international tax treaties for tax litigation evidence, and automating private-equity fund setup. These are concrete project descriptions, not quantified evidence of savings or performance.
qs: a ‘process re-engineering’ project to redefine the way in which lawyers approach and undertake due diligence in corporate M&A;
a tool that iteratively generates reports based on client legal data and international tax treaties, for use as visual evidence in a tax litigation matter;
an automated ‘funds management creation’ platform, to remove the burdensome administrative and manual processes lawyers must ordinarily undertake in the setting up of private equity funds.

kp.k: Crisis workloads highlight scalable contract analysis
kp.d: Freeland reports that Hogan Lovells used existing platforms to review force majeure clauses during the early Covid-19 shutdown. She also describes Dechert and Hogan Lovells developing tools for the anticipated replacement of Libor after 2021, involving millions of legacy deals. Her argument that firms without developed technology were disadvantaged is a contemporary assessment, not a controlled outcome study.
qs: In recent weeks legal engineers have been using the platforms that Hogan Lovells built to review force majeure clauses in contracts that could be triggered by the global Covid-19 shutdown.

Dechert and Hogan Lovells have recently developed their own tools to handle the enormous task faced by banks and other financial institutions in adapting to the (as yet undecided) new benchmark that will replace Libor after 2021.
Without such tools, clients face a Herculean struggle to review millions of legacy deals and update new ones to take account of Libor transition measures.

kp.k: Reusable tools extend innovation across practice areas
kp.d: Freeland describes technology teams' cross-practice perspective as enabling reuse, citing firm-wide deployment of Kira Systems at Dechert. She reports that Linklaters' ISDA Create was used by more than 50 banks to negotiate and execute derivatives documentation while capturing document data. Luke Martin-Fuller emphasises repeatable processes as a route to efficiency.
qs: For example, Dechert’s tech team recently enabled the application of the machine learning contract analysis tool Kira Systems within the entire firm.

He helped to develop ISDA Create, a time-saving online platform used by more than 50 banks to negotiate and execute derivatives documentation, while allowing businesses to capture and process data within the documents.
Once you have set up a process, you can use it again and again
The goal is to create efficiencies.

kp.k: Engineering capabilities broaden firms' competitive service proposition
kp.d: Osborne Clarke's Dan Wright argues that law firms must offer services beyond law, pointing to the Big Four's earlier recognition of such inputs. Dechert partner Sarah Smith presents internal tool-building as valuable to clients and an alternative to expensive external AI vendors. Freeland reports that Simmons & Simmons acquired Wavelength to strengthen data science, technology and design capabilities; these accounts describe strategic rationales, not measured competitive gains.
qs: Law firms have to provide a style of professional service to clients that goes beyond the law
The Big Four realised the value of such inputs 20 years ago.

Being able to turn to the technology team to build in-house tools which address specific client issues, rather than outsourcing to expensive AI vendors, is rare in the legal market, and of real value to clients
It was acquired by Simmons & Simmons last year to enhance its capability to use data science, technology and design on projects.

kp.k: Hybrid skills require legal understanding and continuous learning
kp.d: Martin-Fuller stresses legal-process knowledge, with Freeland also identifying creativity and persuasiveness in translating requirements for software engineers. Wavelength's Erika Pagano emphasises active learning and creative risk-taking. Lilley treats existing Excel, coding or AI-tool knowledge as advantageous but learnable, and recommends developing a data-oriented perspective alongside practical knowledge of solicitors' work.
qs: You need the hard skills – the knowledge of how legal process works and the background legal understanding
You have to be willing to delve deep and take creative risks
It is important to be an active learner.
It will obviously still be an added bonus if you already have excellent Excel skills or have some knowledge of coding languages or AI tools.
Knowing what solicitors do day-to-day and the procedures and documents they interact with regularly is crucial.

kp.k: Recruitment shortages prompt retraining and educational experimentation
kp.d: Freeland reports a shortage of experienced legal engineers despite some trainee coding and technology instruction. Hogan Lovells' Katja Ullrich-North describes recruiting adjacent skill sets and moving people into technology roles. Anna Donovan reports emerging law-school technology curricula and planned firm partnerships for practical experience, arguing that legal engineering warrants high-calibre professionals rather than adjunct status. Equivalent remuneration to legal practice is explicitly described as anecdotal.
qs: Although in many firms trainees are encouraged to learn coding and receive some tech training, experienced legal engineers are in short supply.
What we try to do is find the closest skill set and migrate these into a legal tech role.
Initiatives such as partnering with major law firms so that students can get hands-on experience and mentoring as legal engineers are planned
The legal engineer is not just an adjunct to traditional legal work
with the (anecdotal) prospect of the equivalent remuneration to working as a lawyer.

kp.k: Alternative careers offer flexibility but resist premature formalisation
kp.d: Freeland presents legal engineering as a route outside rigid legal-practice milestones, encompassing training, product research and management-level innovation as well as project work. Dechert's Thor Alden describes permission to experiment outside the traditional legal structure. Stephen Allen cautions that formalising the role could undermine its flexibility and creativity; this is a stated risk, not an observed causal finding.
qs: Many do more than strict ‘legal engineering’, fielding tech-related queries, training lawyers, doing product research or pushing the innovation agenda at management committee meetings, as well as collaborating on transformative projects.
The role is varied and also groundbreaking – we are encouraged to try new things even if they don’t work out at first.
Formalising the role could kill the flexibility and creativity that people enjoy.

kp.k: Client understanding remains an adoption barrier
kp.d: Lilley identifies, explicitly as his personal opinion, difficulty communicating what legal engineering can accomplish. He argues that explaining available solutions helps clients articulate requirements and recommends greater effort to educate clients about deployment, rather than treating technological capability alone as sufficient.
qs: In my personal opinion, I think clients generally find it difficult to understand what we can really do.
Once we explain this to them, it’s usually easy to help them tell us exactly what they want.
All this means is that we have to put more effort making people and our clients aware of what is available and how they can deploy these technologies in the best way possible.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The sources describe technology-enabled legal engineering, including selective use of machine learning and in-house AI, as improving legal workflows rather than replacing lawyers with autonomous systems.
pts.d: Katharine Freeland claims that legal engineering makes legal processes faster, cheaper, more accurate and less labour-intensive. She reports firm-wide deployment of Kira's machine-learning contract analysis at Dechert and development of tools for Libor-related contract work at Dechert and Hogan Lovells. Sarah Smith, interviewed in Freeland's article, claims that building tools internally for specific client problems offers value compared with outsourcing to expensive AI vendors. Will Lilley describes Wavelength's service as identifying inefficiencies in lawyers' procedures and implementing improved processes through collaboration among lawyers, legal engineers and data scientists. The SCL article's organisational profile states that Wavelength can deploy bespoke code and proprietary AI where necessary. These are claims about a broader legal-engineering model: the document does not establish that every described automation project uses AI. Freeland also describes legal engineering as an emerging alternative career with shortages of experienced practitioners; this is a technology-related professional change, not a prediction of lawyer displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Support consists of practitioner experience, named implementations and a regulatory record, not quantified AI performance or causal productivity studies.
pts.d: Freeland supports the efficiency narrative with reported uses of technology: force-majeure contract review at Hogan Lovells, Kira deployment at Dechert, Libor-transition tools and Linklaters' ISDA Create platform, reportedly used by more than 50 banks. The bank count indicates reported adoption, not measured time savings. The SCL interview introduction lists Lilley's recent projects: redesigning M&A due diligence, generating tax-litigation reports from client data and treaties, and automating administrative processes involved in private-equity fund creation. Lilley's account provides first-hand descriptions of multidisciplinary delivery and iterative client feedback. Neither article supplies comparative costs, hours saved, error rates, model benchmarks or staffing reductions. The SRA register confirms licensed-body status since 1 June 2016 and authorisation for legal services; it does not substantiate efficiency claims or independently establish Wavelength's claimed world-first status. Freeland explicitly labels potential lawyer-equivalent remuneration anecdotal.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern capabilities already being deployed in the 2016–2021 period, with near-term predictions tied to Covid-19 and Libor transition; benefits depend on appropriate expertise, workflow design and client understanding.
pts.d: Freeland's article is dated 4 May 2020. Its forecast that only technologically agile firms are likely to mitigate pandemic disruption concerns the following months, and its Libor discussion anticipates replacement of the benchmark after 2021. The supplied compilation places the SCL interview in 2021, although the excerpt itself displays only the relative label '5 years ago'. Wavelength is described as established in 2016 and acquired by Simmons & Simmons in summer 2019. Lilley qualifies the delivery model as technology-agnostic, tailored to the client and supported by small multidisciplinary teams with continuous feedback. He identifies clients' limited understanding of available solutions as an adoption difficulty. AI is described as deployable 'where necessary', not as a universal ingredient. The sources do not offer a timetable for generative AI, autonomous legal practice or occupational replacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries and participants are commercial law firms, institutional clients and multidisciplinary legal-delivery teams; the sources also identify new career opportunities and recruitment constraints.
pts.d: Banks and financial institutions are presented as benefiting from tools for reviewing large volumes of legacy contracts and handling derivatives documentation. Corporate M&A, private-equity fund formation and tax litigation are additional application areas. Law firms gain internal capacity to respond to client demands and reuse solutions across practices; Freeland says firms lacking previously developed technology are disadvantaged during the pandemic. Lawyers' administrative and review processes are redesigned, while legal engineers bridge legal practice and technical implementation. Lilley describes teams of five or six that can include legal engineers, data scientists, technologists, lawyers and designers. Freeland reports alternative career paths for lawyers and opportunities for law students, alongside difficulty recruiting people with combined legal and technical knowledge. The document does not claim a measured loss of junior-lawyer jobs, a change in associate leverage or improvements in access to justice for underserved individuals.
